P(a).name: Measurement probability
P(a).description: The probability of obtaining eigenvalue or outcome a upon measuring an observable.

|a\\rangle.name: Eigenstate vector
|a\\rangle.description: Normalized eigenvector of the measured observable corresponding to outcome a.

|\\psi\\rangle.name: State vector
|\\psi\\rangle.description: Normalized state vector describing the quantum system in Hilbert space.

born-probability-rule-0259a5dd.interpretation: In the expression $P(a) = |\langle a | \psi \rangle|^2$, the term $|\psi\rangle$ represents the normalized state vector of the quantum physical system. The bra $\langle a|$ represents the Hermitian adjoint of the orthonormal eigenstate $|a\rangle$ associated with a measurement outcome $a$. The complex scalar $\langle a | \psi \rangle$ is the probability amplitude, whose modulus squared $|\cdot|^2$ yields the dimensionless probability $P(a) \in [0, 1]$, satisfying $\sum_a P(a) = 1$ under complete basis expansions.
born-probability-rule-0259a5dd.symmetry_origin: Rooted in $U(1)$ global phase invariance and the unitary symmetry $\mathrm{U}(\mathcal{H})$ of the Hilbert space, ensuring the conservation of total probability under unitary time evolution via Gleason's theorem.
born-probability-rule-0259a5dd.limits_and_boundary: In the classical limit $\hbar \to 0$ or via environmental decoherence, off-diagonal interference terms vanish, and the quantum probability distribution reduces asymptotically to a classical statistical ensemble over phase space trajectories.
born-probability-rule-0259a5dd.conceptual_definition: The Born rule connects the abstract state vector $|\psi\rangle$ in a complex Hilbert space to physical observables. For an observable with a non-degenerate discrete eigenstate $|a\rangle$, the probability $P(a)$ of measuring eigenvalue $a$ is defined as $P(a) = |\langle a | \psi \rangle|^2 = \langle \psi | a \rangle \langle a | \psi \rangle = \langle \psi | \hat{P}_a | \psi \rangle$, where $\hat{P}_a = |a\rangle\langle a|$ is the projection operator onto that subspace.
born-probability-rule-0259a5dd.intuitive_summary: Quantum states evolve as complex wave amplitudes; the Born rule acts as the bridge to classical reality by taking the absolute square of this amplitude, translating wave superposition into observable statistical frequencies.
born-probability-rule-0259a5dd.description: Fundamental postulate of quantum mechanics establishing that the probability of obtaining a specific measurement outcome is given by the squared modulus of the projection between the system state and the corresponding eigenstate.

response-factor-60a483ce.description: Defines the linear macroscopic constitutive relation connecting the magnetic flux density to the auxiliary magnetic field intensity via the scalar magnetic permeability of the medium.

flow-regime-4e7283f1.symmetry_origin: Scale invariance and dimensional homogeneity of the Navier-Stokes equations under spatio-temporal rescaling $(\mathbf{x} \to L\tilde{\mathbf{x}}, \mathbf{v} \to v\tilde{\mathbf{v}})$.

In the limit $\mathrm{Re} \to \infty$, viscous dissipation scales down to singular boundary layers, asymptotically recovering the Euler equations of inviscid flow.
flow-regime-4e7283f1.conceptual_definition: The Reynolds number $\mathrm{Re} = \frac{\rho v L}{\\beta}$ emerges naturally from non-dimensionalizing the Navier-Stokes momentum equations. It compares the characteristic scale of fluid inertial acceleration $\rho (\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla)\mathbf{v} \sim \rho v^2 / L$ to the scale of viscous diffusion $\\beta \nabla^2 \mathbf{v} \sim \eta v / L^2$, serving as the primary control parameter for geometric and dynamic similitude in Newtonian fluid flows.

flow-regime-4e7283f1.description: A dimensionless quantity measuring the ratio of convective inertial forces to viscous shear forces in fluid mechanics, governing hydrodynamic similarity and the transition from laminar to turbulent flow regimes.

redshift-source-e7ab2e1d.interpretation: The quantity $1+z$ is the cosmological redshift factor. The term $\lambda_{\text{obs}}/\lambda_{\text{emit}}$ represents the ratio of the wavelength observed at time $t_{\text{now}}$ to the wavelength emitted at time $t_{\text{then}}$. The ratio $a(t_{\text{now}})/a(t_{\text{then}})$ expresses the relative expansion of space between emission and observation epochs. When $a(t_{\text{now}}) > a(t_{\text{then}})$, $z > 0$, indicating a cosmological redshift.
redshift-source-e7ab2e1d.symmetry_origin: Spatial homogeneity and isotropy of the spatial slices in the Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker metric (isometry group $SO(3)$ and spatial translations), preserving null geodesic intervals.
redshift-source-e7ab2e1d.limits_and_boundary: In a static spacetime where $a(t_{\text{now}}) = a(t_{\text{then}})$, $z = 0$ and $\lambda_{\text{obs}} = \lambda_{\text{emit}}$. For light emitted at the Big Bang singularity as $a(t_{\text{then}}) \to 0$, $z \to \infty$ and $\lambda_{\text{obs}} \to \infty$. For infinitesimal lookback times $\Delta t = t_{\text{now}} - t_{\text{then}} \to 0$, the relation reduces to the linear Hubble-Lemaître law $z \approx H_0 \Delta t$.
redshift-source-e7ab2e1d.conceptual_definition: In an isotropic and homogeneous expanding universe described by the FLRW metric, light traveling along null geodesics ($ds^2 = 0$) experiences a wavelength stretching proportional to the expansion of space. The cosmological redshift parameter $z$ is defined via the ratio of observed wavelength $\lambda_{\text{obs}}$ to emitted wavelength $\lambda_{\text{emit}}$, which directly equals the ratio of the scale factor at the epoch of observation $a(t_{\text{now}})$ to that at the epoch of emission $a(t_{\text{then}})$.
redshift-source-e7ab2e1d.intuitive_summary: As photons travel across the cosmos, the expanding fabric of space stretches their wavelengths proportionally to the universe's cosmic scale factor.
redshift-source-e7ab2e1d.description: Relates the observed-to-emitted wavelength ratio of photons propagating across an expanding Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) spacetime to the cosmological redshift and the ratio of cosmic scale factors.

the-recoil-e144c828.interpretation: The symbol $\sigma(pp \to \chi\chi + X)$ denotes the total inclusive production cross section for the process $pp \to \chi\chi + X$, quantifying the effective area or likelihood of generating a pair of dark matter particles $\chi\chi$ accompanied by initial-state or recoil radiation $X$ in proton-proton collisions. The operator $\propto$ represents proportionality. The parameter $g_{\chi\text{SM}}$ is the dimensionless effective coupling constant parametrizing the interaction vertex between the dark sector state $\chi$ and the relevant Standard Model fields (quarks or gluons). Because transition matrix elements $\mathcal{M}$ are linear in the interaction vertex coupling at leading order, the cross section scales as $|\mathcal{M}|^2 \propto g_{\chi\text{SM}}^2$.
the-recoil-e144c828.symmetry_origin: Governed by $S$-matrix unitarity, relativistic Lorentz invariance in quantum field theory, and underlying gauge symmetries ($SU(3)_C \times SU(2)_L \times U(1)_Y$) constraining effective dark matter-Standard Model interaction operators.
the-recoil-e144c828.limits_and_boundary: In the decoupled limit where $g_{\chi\text{SM}} \to 0$, the production cross section vanishes identically: $\lim_{g_{\chi\text{SM}} \to 0} \sigma(pp \to \chi\chi + X) = 0$. When the center-of-mass energy $\sqrt{s} < 2 m_\chi$, phase space closes and $\sigma = 0$. In the non-perturbative regime $g_{\chi\text{SM}} \gg 4\pi$, tree-level proportionality breaks down due to higher-order loop corrections and unitarity violation.
the-recoil-e144c828.conceptual_definition: In high-energy collider physics and dark matter phenomenology, the total or differential cross section for pair-producing weakly interacting massive particles or other dark sector candidates $\chi$ alongside Standard Model radiation $X$ (such as mono-jets, mono-photons, or mono-$Z$) scales quadratically with the fundamental interaction vertex coupling $g_{\chi\text{SM}}$ in the single-mediator or contact interaction regime: $\sigma(pp \to \chi\chi + X) \propto g_{\chi\text{SM}}^2$.
the-recoil-e144c828.intuitive_summary: The probability of creating dark matter particles at a particle accelerator grows with the square of how strongly dark matter talks to ordinary quarks and gluons, following Fermi's Golden Rule.
the-recoil-e144c828.description: Parametric scaling relation for the inclusive production cross section of dark matter pairs in proton-proton collisions with respect to the effective dark matter-Standard Model coupling constant.

the-spectrum-6f5e3c9c.title: Group Velocity

v_g.name: Group Velocity
v_g.description: The velocity of the envelope of a wave packet, representing the speed of energy or information propagation.

\\omega.name: Angular Frequency
\\omega.description: The rate of change of the wave's phase, equal to $2\pi$ times the frequency.

k.name: Wavenumber
k.description: The spatial frequency of the wave, equal to $2\pi$ divided by the wavelength $\lambda$.

\\frac{d}{dk}.name: Derivative with respect to Wavenumber
\\frac{d}{dk}.description: An operator that calculates the rate of change of a function (here, $\omega$) with respect to the wavenumber $k$.

the-spectrum-6f5e3c9c.interpretation: The equation $v_g = \frac{d\omega}{dk}$ quantifies the group velocity ($v_g$), the speed at which the envelope of a wave packet propagates. A wave packet is a localized wave disturbance resulting from the superposition of multiple waves with a narrow range of frequencies and wave numbers. The angular frequency $\omega$ describes the temporal oscillation of the wave, while the wave number $k$ describes its spatial oscillation ($k = 2\pi/\lambda$, where $\lambda$ is the wavelength). The derivative $\frac{d\omega}{dk}$ represents the slope of the dispersion relation, $\omega(k)$, which dictates how the wave's frequency depends on its wave number. In a non-dispersive medium (e.g., light in a vacuum), $\omega$ is linearly proportional to $k$, and the group velocity equals the phase velocity ($v_p = \omega/k$). In a dispersive medium (e.g., light in glass or water waves), this relationship is non-linear, causing $v_g$ to differ from $v_p$ and leading to the spreading of the wave packet over time.
the-spectrum-6f5e3c9c.symmetry_origin: The concept of group velocity arises from the principle of superposition, which is valid for linear wave equations. The underlying symmetries of these equations (e.g., Lorentz invariance for electromagnetism, Galilean invariance for non-relativistic quantum mechanics) determine the specific form of the dispersion relation $\omega(k)$.
the-spectrum-6f5e3c9c.limits_and_boundary: In the non-dispersive limit, where $\omega(k) = c k$, the group velocity $v_g = \frac{d(ck)}{dk} = c$, which equals the phase velocity $v_p$. For a non-relativistic free particle with mass $m$, the de Broglie relations ($E=\hbar\omega$, $p=\hbar k$) and the kinetic energy formula ($E=p^2/2m$) yield the dispersion relation $\omega(k) = \frac{\hbar k^2}{2m}$. The group velocity is then $v_g = \frac{d\omega}{dk} = \frac{\hbar k}{m} = \frac{p}{m}$, which is precisely the classical velocity of the particle. In all physical media, the group velocity, representing the speed of information, is bounded by the speed of light in vacuum, $v_g \le c$.
the-spectrum-6f5e3c9c.conceptual_definition: For a wave packet formed by the superposition of plane waves, the group velocity $v_g$ is defined as the derivative of the angular frequency $\omega$ with respect to the wave number $k$. This relationship, $v_g = d\omega/dk$, is evaluated at the central wave number of the packet and describes the speed of the overall amplitude modulation, distinct from the speed of the individual phase crests.
the-spectrum-6f5e3c9c.intuitive_summary: Imagine a traffic jam on a highway. The speed of individual cars moving through the jam is the 'phase velocity', while the speed at which the jam itself moves along the highway is the 'group velocity'. For waves, the group velocity is the speed of the 'bunch' or 'packet' of energy.
the-spectrum-6f5e3c9c.description: Defines the group velocity as the propagation speed of the envelope of a wave packet, which corresponds to the speed of energy and information transfer in a dispersive medium.

star-fall-2c9ddfb7.title: Temporal Variation Limit of the Gravitational Constant

\\delta G.name: Change in Gravitational Constant
\\delta G.description: The change in the value of Newton's gravitational constant over a specified time interval, typically one year for this expression.

G.name: Newtonian Gravitational Constant
G.description: The empirical physical constant quantifying the magnitude of the gravitational force between two bodies. Its constancy is being tested.

\\delta.name: Variation Operator
\\delta.description: Represents a small change or variation in a physical quantity. In this context, it implies a change over time, often denoted as a time derivative $\dot{G}$.

\\text{year}.name: Year
\\text{year}.description: A unit of time, defined as the period of Earth's orbit around the Sun, used here as the timescale for the potential variation.

star-fall-2c9ddfb7.interpretation: The formula $\delta G / G < 10^{-12} \text{ /year}$ is an observational constraint on physical theories. The term $\delta G$ represents the change in the gravitational constant over a one-year time interval, while $G$ is the current accepted value of the gravitational constant. The ratio $\delta G / G$, often written as $\dot{G}/G$, quantifies the fractional or relative change in $G$ per year. The inequality sets an experimental upper bound on this fractional change, indicating that any variation must be smaller than one part in $10^{12}$ annually. This result strongly supports theories where fundamental constants are truly constant, like General Relativity, and constrains alternative theories like Brans-Dicke theory where $G$ can vary.
star-fall-2c9ddfb7.symmetry_origin: This experimental constraint tests the validity of the Strong Equivalence Principle (SEP), which is a foundational assumption of General Relativity. In theories that satisfy the SEP, the gravitational constant $G$ is a true universal constant. A non-zero value for $\dot{G}/G$ would indicate a violation of the SEP and imply new scalar fields, as predicted in alternative theories of gravity.
star-fall-2c9ddfb7.limits_and_boundary: This inequality acts as a strong constraint on cosmological models and theories of gravity. In the limit of a theory where the Strong Equivalence Principle holds exactly, one would expect $\delta G / G = 0$. This experimental bound forces any viable alternative theory of gravity (e.g., scalar-tensor theories) to have parameters that make the variation of $G$ extremely small in the current cosmological epoch, effectively behaving like General Relativity.
star-fall-2c9ddfb7.conceptual_definition: This inequality represents a fundamental test of the strong equivalence principle, a cornerstone of general relativity. It posits that the gravitational constant, $G$, is a true universal constant and does not vary with time or location. The expression $\delta G / G$ represents the fractional change in $G$ over a given period. The value $10^{-12}$ per year is an extremely stringent upper limit established by high-precision experiments, such as lunar laser ranging and observations of binary pulsar systems.
star-fall-2c9ddfb7.intuitive_summary: Imagine the force of gravity is controlled by a universal 'gravity knob'. This formula tells us that if this knob is being turned at all, it's turning incredibly slowly—less than one part in a trillion per year. For all practical purposes, the strength of gravity is constant everywhere and for all time.
star-fall-2c9ddfb7.description: An experimental upper bound on the fractional rate of change of Newton's gravitational constant ($G$), derived from astrophysical observations and tests of the strong equivalence principle.

technical-relation-39ff4117.interpretation: The Hubble parameter $H(t)$ describes the time-dependent relative expansion rate of the cosmos with physical units of inverse time ($\text{s}^{-1}$). The parameter $t$ represents the cosmic proper time elapsed since the initial singularity ($t = 0$). technical-relation-39ff4117.symmetry_origin: Derived under the assumption of the Cosmological Principle (spatial homogeneity and isotropy), described by the Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) metric and local conservation of the stress-energy tensor $\nabla_\mu T^{\mu\nu} = 0$.
technical-relation-39ff4117.limits_and_boundary: As $t \to 0$, $H(t) \to \infty$, reflecting the Big Bang curvature singularity. As $t \to \infty$, $H(t) \to 0$, representing asymptotic deceleration towards static expansion in the absence of a cosmological constant or dark energy.
technical-relation-39ff4117.conceptual_definition: In standard cosmological models governed by General Relativity, a flat ($k = 0$) universe dominated by non-relativistic cold matter (dust with equation-of-state parameter $w = 0$) exhibits a scale factor scaling as $a(t) \propto t^{2/3}$. The instantaneous expansion rate, quantified by the Hubble parameter $H(t) \equiv \dot{a}/a$, is inversely proportional to the cosmic time $t$ via the relation $H(t) = \frac{2}{3t}$.

time-dependent-identity-f7492328.title: Time-Dependent Schrödinger Equation in Dirac Notation

time-dependent-identity-f7492328.interpretation: The state ket $|\psiangle$ represents the complete quantum state of the physical system in Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$. On the left-hand side, $i$ is the imaginary unit, $\hbar$ is the reduced Planck constant, and $\frac{\partial}{\partial t}$ denotes the partial derivative with respect to time coordinate $t$. The term $i\hbar \frac{\partial}{\partial t}|\psiangle$ characterizes the dynamical rate of phase and state evolution. On the right-hand side, $\hat{H}$ is the self-adjoint Hamiltonian operator representing the total energy observable of the system. Its action $\hat{H}|\psiangle$ dictates the instantaneous trajectory and phase rotation of the quantum state.
time-dependent-identity-f7492328.symmetry_origin: Originates from continuous time-translation symmetry via Noether's theorem and Stone's theorem on one-parameter unitary groups, where the Hamiltonian $\hat{H}$ serves as the self-adjoint generator of unitary time evolution $U(t) = \exp(-i\hat{H}t/\hbar)$.
time-dependent-identity-f7492328.limits_and_boundary: In the semiclassical limit ($\hbar \to 0$), the equation yields the classical Hamilton-Jacobi equation via the WKB approximation. For stationary states where $\hat{H}|\psiangle = E|\psiangle$, the time evolution factors into a harmonic phase factor $e^{-iEt/\hbar}$. In relativistic regimes ($v \to c$), the equation must be generalized to the Klein-Gordon or Dirac equations.
time-dependent-identity-f7492328.conceptual_definition: The Time-Dependent Schrödinger Equation (TDSE) is the quantum mechanical equation of motion postulating that the rate of change of a quantum state $|\psiangle$ with respect to time $t$ is directly proportional to the action of the Hamiltonian operator $\hat{H}$ on that state. In the abstract Hilbert space formulation, it dictates that the generator of infinitesimal time translations is given by $\hat{H}/\hbar$, ensuring the preservation of probability norms under unitary dynamics.
time-dependent-identity-f7492328.intuitive_summary: Just as Newton's second law governs the trajectory of classical bodies, the Schrödinger equation determines how the quantum probability amplitude rotates and evolves through Hilbert space under the influence of the system's total energy operator.
time-dependent-identity-f7492328.description: The fundamental postulate of non-relativistic quantum mechanics governing the deterministic and unitary time evolution of a quantum state vector in Hilbert space.

atomic-magnet-13cf87c1.interpretation: The quantity $\mu_B$ is the Bohr magneton (measured in $\text{J}\cdot\text{T}^{-1}$ or $\text{A}\cdot\text{m}^2$). The parameter $e$ is the elementary charge ($1.602 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$), denoting the fundamental electric coupling constant. The reduced Planck constant $\hbar$ ($1.055 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J}\cdot\text{s}$) defines the quantum scale of action and angular momentum. The denominator contains $m_e$, the electron rest mass ($9.109 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}$), and a factor of $2$ arising from the classical-to-quantum correspondence of the gyromagnetic ratio for orbital motion.
atomic-magnet-13cf87c1.symmetry_origin: $U(1)$ electromagnetic gauge invariance coupled with $SO(3)$ rotational symmetry governing angular momentum quantization in non-relativistic limits of the Dirac equation.
atomic-magnet-13cf87c1.limits_and_boundary: In the classical limit $\hbar \to 0$, the quantization scale vanishes, allowing continuous orbital magnetic moments $\boldsymbol{\mu} \to 0$. In the ultra-relativistic regime $v \to c$, magnetic moments require full quantum electrodynamic radiative vertex corrections via the anomalous magnetic dipole moment $(g-2)$.
atomic-magnet-13cf87c1.conceptual_definition: The Bohr magneton $\mu_B = \frac{e \hbar}{2 m_e}$ represents the magnitude of the magnetic dipole moment associated with an electron having an orbital angular momentum of one unit of reduced Planck constant $\hbar$. It serves as the standard physical constant characterizing atomic-scale magnetic phenomena and electron spin-orbit coupling.
atomic-magnet-13cf87c1.intuitive_summary: Think of the electron as a circulating quantum charge whose minimal non-zero angular momentum quantizes the strength of the magnetic field it can generate into discrete natural units.
atomic-magnet-13cf87c1.description: Defines the fundamental natural unit of magnetic dipole moment for an electron, emerging from the quantization of orbital angular momentum and Dirac relativistic quantum mechanics.

consistency-guide-04209475.title: Law of Total Probability

P(A).name: Marginal Probability of Event A
P(A).description: Total probability of occurrence of event or observation $A$

P(H_i).name: Prior Probability of Hypothesis
P(H_i).description: Prior probability assigned to the $i$-th hypothesis or partition element $H_i$

P(A|H_i).name: Conditional Probability
P(A|H_i).description: Probability of event $A$ conditional upon the truth of hypothesis $H_i$

consistency-guide-04209475.interpretation: In this equation, $P(A)$ represents the total or marginal probability of event $A$. The summation runs over an index $i$ corresponding to a partition of hypotheses $\{H_i\}$. The term $P(H_i)$ is the prior or marginal probability of the $i$-th hypothesis, while $P(A|H_i)$ is the conditional probability (likelihood) of observing event $A$ given that hypothesis $H_i$ holds true.
consistency-guide-04209475.symmetry_origin: Originates from the $\sigma$-additivity axiom of probability measure spaces (Kolmogorov axioms) under partition invariance.
consistency-guide-04209475.limits_and_boundary: If the partition consists of a single certainty $H_1 = \Omega$, then $P(H_1) = 1$ and the expression reduces trivially to $P(A) = P(A|\Omega)$. In continuous hypothesis spaces, the summation transitions to an integral over the parameter space: $P(A) = \int P(H) P(A|H) dH$.
consistency-guide-04209475.conceptual_definition: Given a sample space $\Omega$ partitioned into a countable collection of pairwise disjoint events $\{H_i\}$ such that $\bigcup_i H_i = \Omega$ and $P(H_i) > 0$ for all $i$, the total probability of any event $A \subseteq \Omega$ is given by $P(A) = \sum_i P(H_i) P(A|H_i)$. This serves as the fundamental consistency condition for marginalization and evidence normalization in Bayesian inference and statistical mechanics.
consistency-guide-04209475.intuitive_summary: To find the overall chance of an event occurring, sum up the chances of each distinct scenario happening multiplied by how likely the event is within that specific scenario.
consistency-guide-04209475.description: The law of total probability expresses the marginal probability of an event as the sum of its conditional probabilities across a complete set of mutually exclusive and exhaustive hypotheses.

degeneracy-condition-6658ae1f.title: Degenerate Vacuum Condition in Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking

\\mathcal{G}/\\mathcal{H}.name: Vacuum Manifold Coset Space
\\mathcal{G}/\\mathcal{H}.description: Homogeneous space parameterizing physically distinct but degenerate vacuum states

degeneracy-condition-6658ae1f.interpretation: Here, $V(\phi)$ denotes the scalar potential energy density as a function of the field configuration $\phi$. The state $\phi_{\text{min}}$ represents any configuration within the vacuum manifold that minimizes $V(\phi)$. The group $\mathcal{G}$ represents the continuous global symmetry group of the Lagrangian, while $\mathcal{H}$ is the isotropy (little) group leaving a chosen vacuum expectation value invariant. The coset space $\mathcal{G}/\mathcal{H}$ represents the vacuum manifold (Goldstone manifold), and $V_0$ is the constant minimum energy density shared by all degenerate vacua.
degeneracy-condition-6658ae1f.symmetry_origin: Global continuous group invariance $\mathcal{G}$ of the potential $V(g \cdot \phi) = V(\phi)$, which naturally induces a constant value of the potential along the orbit of any minimum state under the action of the coset $\mathcal{G}/\mathcal{H}$.
degeneracy-condition-6658ae1f.limits_and_boundary: In the limit of explicit symmetry breaking (e.g., adding an external field or perturbation $\epsilon \Delta V$), the degeneracy is lifted, and the coset manifold $\mathcal{G}/\mathcal{H}$ ceases to be equipotential, yielding pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone bosons with non-zero mass.
degeneracy-condition-6658ae1f.conceptual_definition: In classical field theories and quantum field theories featuring spontaneous symmetry breaking, an invariant potential $V(\phi)$ under a global symmetry group $\mathcal{G}$ possesses a set of degenerate global minima $\phi_{\text{min}}$. When the vacuum expectation value is invariant only under a subgroup $\mathcal{H} \subset \mathcal{G}$, the vacuum manifold forms the homogeneous space (coset space) $\mathcal{M}_0 \cong \mathcal{G}/\mathcal{H}$, upon which the potential energy is identically equal to the ground-state energy density $V_0$.
degeneracy-condition-6658ae1f.intuitive_summary: The bottom of the potential well forms a continuous, flat valley (like the circular trough of a Mexican-hat potential) where any state in the valley has the exact same lowest energy.
degeneracy-condition-6658ae1f.description: States that the scalar potential attains an identical global minimum value across the entire coset manifold $\mathcal{G}/\mathcal{H}$, characterizing degenerate vacuum ground states in spontaneous symmetry breaking.

\\Phi_0.name: Magnetic Flux Quantum
\\Phi_0.description: Fundamental quantum of magnetic flux in a superconductor

e.name: Elementary Charge
e.description: Magnitude of electric charge carried by a single electron

flux-quantum-52e84a54.interpretation: In the relation $\Phi_0 = \frac{h}{2e}$, $\Phi_0$ denotes the magnetic flux quantum measured in Webers ($\text{Wb} = \text{V}\cdot\text{s}$). The numerator $h$ is Planck's constant, dictating the quantum of action. The denominator contains $2e$, which represents the effective electric charge $q^* = 2e$ of a Cooper pair formed by two electrons each carrying the elementary charge $e$. The quantization condition $\oint \nabla \theta \cdot d\mathbf{l} = 2\pi n$ directly implies that the trapped magnetic flux $\Phi = \oint \mathbf{A} \cdot d\mathbf{l}$ must be an integer multiple $n \Phi_0$.
flux-quantum-52e84a54.symmetry_origin: $U(1)$ electromagnetic gauge invariance combined with the macroscopic phase coherence of the Ginzburg-Landau condensate order parameter.
flux-quantum-52e84a54.limits_and_boundary: In the classical limit $\hbar \to 0$, the flux quantum $\Phi_0 \to 0$, recovering continuous magnetic flux behavior. Above the superconducting critical temperature $T > T_c$ or upper critical magnetic field $B > B_{c2}$, Cooper pairing is destroyed, macroscopic phase coherence is lost, and magnetic flux quantization ceases to hold.
flux-quantum-52e84a54.conceptual_definition: The superconducting flux quantum $\Phi_0 = \frac{h}{2e}$ is the intrinsic quantum unit of magnetic flux enclosed by a multiply connected superconductor. It arises from the single-valuedness requirement of the macroscopic superconducting order parameter $\psi(\mathbf{r}) = \sqrt{n_s} e^{i\theta(\mathbf{r})}$ along a closed path where the supercurrent density vanishes deep within the bulk.
flux-quantum-52e84a54.intuitive_summary: Just as electric charge is quantized in units of $e$, magnetic flux penetrating a superconducting ring is quantized in discrete packets of $\Phi_0$, with the factor of 2 reflecting that electrons pair up into Cooper pairs before conducting without resistance.
flux-quantum-52e84a54.description: The magnetic flux quantum represents the fundamental quantum of magnetic flux threading a superconducting loop, determined by the ratio of Planck's constant to the charge of a Cooper pair.

maxwell-faraday-law-identity-1-44ef41b7-.title: The Maxwell-Faraday Law of Induction

maxwell-faraday-law-identity-1-44ef41b7-.interpretation: The left-hand side, $\nabla \times \mathbf{E}$, represents the curl or circulation density of the electric field $\mathbf{E}$. A non-zero curl indicates the presence of a non-electrostatic, non-conservative field whose line integral along a closed path does not vanish. The right-hand side, $-\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t}$, is the negative instantaneous rate of change of the magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$. The negative sign embodies Lenz's law, ensuring that any induced current creates a secondary magnetic field counteracting the original magnetic flux perturbation.
maxwell-faraday-law-identity-1-44ef41b7-.symmetry_origin: Originates from the Bianchi identity of the electromagnetic field strength tensor $dF = 0$ (or $\partial_{[\mu} F_{\nu\lambda]} = 0$), reflecting the underlying $U(1)$ gauge symmetry and the absence of magnetic monopoles.
maxwell-faraday-law-identity-1-44ef41b7-.limits_and_boundary: In the electrostatic/magnetostatic limit ($\frac{\partial}{\partial t} \to 0$), the equation reduces to $\nabla \times \mathbf{E} = \mathbf{0}$, guaranteeing that the electrostatic field is purely conservative and expressible as the gradient of a scalar potential $\mathbf{E} = -\nabla \Phi$.
maxwell-faraday-law-identity-1-44ef41b7-.conceptual_definition: The Maxwell-Faraday equation relates the curl of the electric field $\mathbf{E}$ to the negative partial time derivative of the magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$: $\nabla \times \mathbf{E} = -\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t}$. It serves as the local differential formulation of Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction.
maxwell-faraday-law-identity-1-44ef41b7-.intuitive_summary: Changing magnetic flux dynamically curls the surrounding electric field into closed loops, producing an electromotive force that opposes the change according to Lenz's law.
maxwell-faraday-law-identity-1-44ef41b7-.description: A fundamental Maxwell equation stating that a time-varying magnetic field induces a spatially circulating, non-conservative electric field.

robertson-uncertainty-identity-1-3916496.title: Schrödinger-Robertson Generalized Uncertainty Relation
robertson-uncertainty-identity-1-3916496.interpretation: In this relation, $\sigma_A^2 = \langle \hat{A}^2 \rangle - \langle \hat{A} \rangle^2$ and $\sigma_B^2 = \langle \hat{B}^2 \rangle - \langle \hat{B} \rangle^2$ denote the statistical variances of observables $\hat{A}$ and $\hat{B}$ respectively in a given quantum state $|\psi\rangle$. The commutator $[\hat{A}, \hat{B}] = \hat{A}\hat{B} - \hat{B}\hat{A}$ measures the non-commutativity of the observables, while the anticommutator $\{\hat{A}, \hat{B}\} = \hat{A}\hat{B} + \hat{B}\hat{A}$ determines the quantum symmetrized covariance $\text{Cov}(\hat{A}, \hat{B}) = \frac{1}{2} \langle \{\hat{A}, \hat{B}\} \rangle - \langle \hat{A} \rangle \langle \hat{B} \rangle$. The symbol $\langle \cdot \rangle$ denotes the quantum expectation value $\langle \psi | \cdot | \psi \rangle$.
robertson-uncertainty-identity-1-3916496.symmetry_origin: Rooted in the positive-semidefinite inner-product structure (Cauchy-Schwarz inequality) of complex Hilbert space and the unitary invariance of state vectors under transformation groups generated by Hermitian observables.
robertson-uncertainty-identity-1-3916496.limits_and_boundary: In the classical limit $\hbar \to 0$, quantum commutators vanish ($[\hat{A}, \hat{B}] \to 0$), leaving purely classical statistical covariance $\sigma_A^2 \sigma_B^2 \ge (\text{Cov}(A,B))^2$. When the quantum covariance is zero, the relation reduces exactly to the standard Robertson uncertainty bound $\sigma_A^2 \sigma_B^2 \ge \frac{1}{4} |\langle [\hat{A}, \hat{B}] \rangle|^2$.

\\sigma_A^2.name: Variance of observable A
\\sigma_A^2.description: Statistical variance of the Hermitian operator $\hat{A}$ in state $|\psi\rangle$

\\sigma_B^2.name: Variance of observable B
\\sigma_B^2.description: Statistical variance of the Hermitian operator $\hat{B}$ in state $|\psi\rangle$

\\hat{A}.name: Observable A
\\hat{A}.description: First Hermitian quantum mechanical observable operator

\\hat{B}.name: Observable B
\\hat{B}.description: Second Hermitian quantum mechanical observable operator

robertson-uncertainty-identity-1-3916496.conceptual_definition: The Schrödinger-Robertson relation generalizes the Robertson uncertainty bound by incorporating the quantum covariance term $\frac{1}{2} \langle \{\hat{A}, \hat{B}\} \rangle - \langle \hat{A} \rangle \langle \hat{B} \rangle$. For any two Hermitian operators $\hat{A}$ and $\hat{B}$ acting on a Hilbert space, the product of their statistical variances satisfies $\sigma_A^2 \sigma_B^2 \ge \left| \frac{1}{2} \langle \{\hat{A}, \hat{B}\} \rangle - \langle \hat{A} \rangle \langle \hat{B} \rangle \right|^2 + \frac{1}{4} \left| \langle [\hat{A}, \hat{B}] \rangle \right|^2$, establishing the most comprehensive state-dependent lower bound on simultaneous quantum measurement precision.
robertson-uncertainty-identity-1-3916496.intuitive_summary: While the standard Heisenberg-Robertson uncertainty principle accounts solely for operator non-commutativity, the Schrödinger-Robertson inequality shows that quantum correlation (covariance) between two observables also contributes directly to the irreducible spread in their joint fluctuations.
robertson-uncertainty-identity-1-3916496.description: A fundamental quantum inequality providing a lower bound for the product of variances of two arbitrary Hermitian operators in terms of both their commutator and covariance.

covariant-derivative-of-the-metric-tenso.title: Covariant derivative of the metric tensor is zero
covariant-derivative-of-the-metric-tenso.conceptual_definition: The equation ∇₀ gµ½ = 0, known as the vanishing covariant derivative of the metric tensor, is a fundamental principle in differential geometry and general relativity. It signifies that the metric tensor, which defines the geometry of spacetime (including distances and angles), is 'covariantly constant'. This means that when the metric tensor is differentiated in a way that accounts for the curvature of spacetime (using a covariant derivative), the result is zero. This property is crucial because it implies that the way distances and angles are measured is consistent throughout spacetime, regardless of the chosen coordinate system, and that spacetime is 'flat' in a specific, 'parallel transport' sense, even if it is curved.
covariant-derivative-of-the-metric-tenso.intuitive_summary: The way distances and angles are measured in spacetime remains consistent when moving parallel to oneself, even in curved spacetime.
covariant-derivative-of-the-metric-tenso.interpretation: In this equation, ∇₀ represents the covariant derivative with respect to the Greek index ρ, which is a generalization of the ordinary partial derivative that accounts for the curvature of the manifold. The symbol gµ½ is the metric tensor, a second-rank covariant tensor field that defines the inner product of tangent vectors at each point in spacetime, thus defining the metric of the spacetime. The indices µ and ν are spacetime indices, typically ranging from 0 to 3 in four-dimensional spacetime. The equation ∇₀ gµ½ = 0 states that the metric tensor is covariantly constant. This means that the 'measure' of spacetime, as defined by the metric tensor, does not change intrinsically as one moves through spacetime, provided this movement is done in a parallel manner (which is precisely what the covariant derivative describes). This is a non-trivial statement about the nature of spacetime itself.
covariant-derivative-of-the-metric-tenso.symmetry_origin: The vanishing covariant derivative of the metric tensor is a consequence of the metric compatibility condition. It arises from the requirement that the metric tensor should define a consistent geometric structure throughout the manifold. In the context of general relativity, this condition ensures that the notion of 'distance' and 'angle' is well-defined and does not depend on the specific coordinate system chosen. It's a fundamental property of Levi-Civita connections, which are torsion-free and metric-compatible. The Levi-Civita connection is uniquely determined by the metric tensor, and the condition ∇_ρ g_{µ½} = 0 ensures that the metric tensor is invariant under parallel transport. This invariance is deeply connected to the principle of general covariance, stating that the laws of physics should take the same form in all coordinate systems.
covariant-derivative-of-the-metric-tenso.limits_and_boundary: This equation is generally a statement about the global properties of spacetime and does not typically involve limits in the sense of variables approaching zero or infinity, as it holds true for all points in the manifold under consideration. However, in specific contexts, one might consider limits of the metric tensor itself or its derivatives in certain regions. For instance, in regions far from massive objects, spacetime approaches a flat Minkowski spacetime, where the metric tensor is constant (ηµ½), and its covariant derivative (and hence its ordinary derivative) is trivially zero. Conversely, near singularities, the metric tensor and its derivatives can become singular, and the interpretation of the covariant derivative might require careful consideration of regularization techniques.

\\nabla_\\rho.description: The covariant derivative operator. It generalizes the ordinary partial derivative to curved spaces or manifolds, taking into account the change in basis vectors with position. Here, ρ is the index of the derivative, indicating the direction of differentiation.

It allows us to measure lengths of tangent vectors and angles between them. The indices µ and ν refer to the components of the tensor in a given coordinate system.

hamiltonian-approaches-zero.title: Vanishing Action Quantum / Classical Limit Condition
hamiltonian-approaches-zero.conceptual_definition: The condition $h \to 0$ (or $\hbar \to 0$) denotes the formal mathematical limit in which the quantum of action is treated as negligibly small relative to the characteristic classical action $S$ of the physical system ($S \gg \hbar$). In this regime, quantum wave mechanics transitions asymptotically into classical Hamiltonian or Lagrangian mechanics via the WKB approximation and Ehrenfest's theorem.
hamiltonian-approaches-zero.intuitive_summary: As the fundamental quantum of action shrinks toward zero, quantum uncertainties and phase interference vanish, recovering deterministic classical trajectory mechanics.
hamiltonian-approaches-zero.interpretation: The symbol $h$ represents Planck's constant ($h \approx 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J}\cdot\text{s}$). The operation $h \to 0$ expresses the semiclassical limit where quantum commutation relations $[\hat{x}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$ asymptotically map to classical Poisson brackets $\{x, p\} = 1$, suppressing quantum tunneling and phase coherence across macroscopic scales.
hamiltonian-approaches-zero.symmetry_origin: Deformation quantization and the contraction of the Heisenberg-Weyl Lie algebra into the commutative Poisson algebra of classical observables.
hamiltonian-approaches-zero.limits_and_boundary: In the limit $h \to 0$, path integrals $\int \mathcal{D}x \, e^{iS[x]/\hbar}$ become dominated entirely by stationary phase trajectories $\delta S = 0$, recovering the principle of least action.

h.description: Fundamental quantum of action governing the scale of quantum physical phenomena

hamiltonian-approaches-zero.description: Represents the asymptotic limiting condition where Planck's constant approaches zero, formalizing the classical limit correspondence principle.

hamiltonian-generalized-coords-momenta.title: Hamiltonian Function via Legendre Transformation
hamiltonian-generalized-coords-momenta.equation: H(q, p, t) = \sum_{i} p_i \dot{q}_i - L(q, \dot{q}, t)
hamiltonian-generalized-coords-momenta.conceptual_definition: The Hamiltonian $H(q, p, t)$ represents the total energy formulation of classical mechanics on the cotangent bundle (phase space). It is obtained from the Lagrangian $L(q, \dot{q}, t)$ on the tangent bundle via the fiber derivative (Legendre transformation) $p_i = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{q}_i}$, trading generalized velocities $\dot{q}_i$ for canonical conjugate momenta $p_i$ through the relation $H(q, p, t) = \sum_{i} p_i \dot{q}_i - L(q, \dot{q}, t)$.
hamiltonian-generalized-coords-momenta.intuitive_summary: The Hamiltonian re-expresses the dynamics of a physical system from position-velocity space into position-momentum phase space, converting second-order Euler-Lagrange equations into a symmetric set of first-order canonical differential equations.
hamiltonian-generalized-coords-momenta.interpretation: The quantity $H(q, p, t)$ is the Hamiltonian evaluated on canonical coordinates $(q_i, p_i)$ and time $t$. The index $i$ runs over all $n$ degrees of freedom of the configuration manifold. The term $p_i = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{q}_i}$ denotes the generalized momentum conjugate to coordinate $q_i$, while $\dot{q}_i = \frac{dq_i}{dt}$ is the corresponding generalized velocity. The function $L(q, \dot{q}, t)$ is the system Lagrangian. In systems where the potential energy is velocity-independent and coordinate transformations are scleronomic (time-independent), $H$ simplifies to the total mechanical energy $T + V$.
hamiltonian-generalized-coords-momenta.symmetry_origin: By Noether's theorem, continuous time-translation invariance of the Lagrangian ($\frac{\partial L}{\partial t} = 0$) implies the conservation of the Hamiltonian along the classical trajectory ($\frac{dH}{dt} = 0$), establishing energy conservation.
hamiltonian-generalized-coords-momenta.limits_and_boundary: In the non-relativistic limit with standard quadratic kinetic energy $T = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j} m_{ij}(q) \dot{q}_i \dot{q}_j$ and velocity-independent potential $V(q)$, the Hamiltonian takes the quadratic form $H = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j} (m^{-1})^{ij} p_i p_j + V(q)$. Under singular Lagrangians where $\det(\frac{\partial^2 L}{\partial \dot{q}_i \partial \dot{q}_j}) = 0$, Dirac-Bergmann constraint analysis is required.

cobalt-56-decay-timescale.title: Cobalt-56 Mean Decay Lifetime
cobalt-56-decay-timescale.conceptual_definition: The Cobalt-56 decay timescale $\tau_{\text{Co}}$ is defined as the inverse of its total nuclear transition decay constant $\lambda_{\text{Co}}$, satisfying the exponential decay law $N_{\text{Co}}(t) = N_{\text{Co}}(0) e^{-t / \tau_{\text{Co}}}$. The nucleus decays primarily through electron capture ($81\%$) and $\beta^+$ emission ($19\%$) to excited states of $^{56}\text{Fe}$, releasing $\gamma$-ray lines and positrons that thermalize within expanding supernova ejecta.
cobalt-56-decay-timescale.intuitive_summary: Following the fast initial decay of synthesized Nickel-56, Cobalt-56 acts as a long-lived nuclear battery with a mean lifetime of roughly 111.3 days, dictating the steady, months-long radioactive fading of supernova light curves.
cobalt-56-decay-timescale.interpretation: In the relation $\tau_{\text{Co}} \approx 111.3 \text{ days}$, the symbol $\tau_{\text{Co}}$ represents the nuclear mean lifetime of $^{56}\text{Co}$ in its ground state ($J^\pi = 4^+$). It relates to the half-life via $t_{1/2} = \tau_{\text{Co}} \ln 2 \approx 77.2 \text{ days}$. The numerical value is determined by the Fermi and Gamow-Teller matrix elements of the weak interaction mediating the $\beta^+$/electron capture transition to $^{56}\text{Fe}$.
cobalt-56-decay-timescale.symmetry_origin: Governed by $SU(2)_L \times U(1)_Y$ electroweak gauge symmetry and mediated by the charged weak current ($W^\pm$ exchange) subject to nuclear isospin and angular momentum selection rules.
cobalt-56-decay-timescale.limits_and_boundary: In the limit $t \ll \tau_{\text{Co}}$, the population of $^{56}\text{Co}$ remains approximately constant: $N(t) \approx N_0(1 - t/\tau_{\text{Co}})$. For late times $t \gg \tau_{\text{Co}}$, the population and corresponding radioactive power deposition decay asymptotically to zero as $\exp(-t/\tau_{\text{Co}})$. In fully stripped laboratory environments without bound electrons, the decay rate decreases because the electron capture channel is suppressed, extending $\tau_{\text{Co}}$ to the pure positron emission lifetime.

schwarzschild-radius-cosmological.title: Schwarzschild Radius (Cosmological)
schwarzschild-radius-cosmological.conceptual_definition: The Schwarzschild radius, when applied cosmologically, represents the radius of a hypothetical sphere such that if all the matter within that sphere were compressed to a density equivalent to that of the observable universe, the escape velocity from its surface would equal the speed of light. This concept is often invoked in discussions about the ultimate fate of the universe or the formation of supermassive black holes.
schwarzschild-radius-cosmological.intuitive_summary: It's the distance from which light would need to travel for an entire eon to escape if the universe were concentrated into a single, extremely dense object.
schwarzschild-radius-cosmological.interpretation: The formula, presented as $r_s \approx 147 \text{ Mpc}$, is a simplified approximation of the Schwarzschild radius for the observable universe. The standard formula for the Schwarzschild radius of a black hole is $r_s = \frac{2GM}{c^2}$, where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $M$ is the mass, and $c$ is the speed of light. In the cosmological context, the mass $M$ is taken to be the mass of the observable universe, and $r_s$ is the radius of the observable universe itself. However, this approximation is derived by equating the universe's average density to the critical density required for a flat universe, and then calculating the Schwarzschild radius for that total mass. The value of 147 Megaparsecs (Mpc) is an estimate derived from current cosmological parameters like the Hubble constant and the matter density of the universe.
schwarzschild-radius-cosmological.symmetry_origin: The Schwarzschild radius is fundamentally derived from Einstein's field equations of general relativity, which describe gravity as the curvature of spacetime. It arises from the spherically symmetric vacuum solution to these equations, known as the Schwarzschild metric. The concept is linked to the idea of an event horizon, a boundary in spacetime beyond which events cannot affect an outside observer. In the cosmological context, it relates to the overall geometry and density of the universe.
schwarzschild-radius-cosmological.limits_and_boundary: For a given mass $M$, if $M$ approaches zero, the Schwarzschild radius $r_s$ approaches zero. If $M$ approaches infinity, $r_s$ also approaches infinity. In the cosmological interpretation, the observable universe has a finite mass and radius, leading to a specific, non-zero Schwarzschild radius. If the universe's average density were to increase significantly, the calculated cosmological Schwarzschild radius would decrease, potentially implying a future collapse if it were to reach the actual radius of the universe.

power-of-exhaust.title: Kinetic Jet Power of Rocket Exhaust
power-of-exhaust.conceptual_definition: The kinetic exhaust power $P$ is the time rate of change of the kinetic energy imparted to the propellant mass flow in the reference frame of the rocket. Assuming steady, one-dimensional, and uniform ejection of exhaust gas at constant effective velocity $v_e$, the power delivered into the exhaust plume is $P = \frac{dE_k}{dt} = \frac{1}{2} \dot{m} v_e^2$.
power-of-exhaust.intuitive_summary: Rocket propulsion converts stored chemical or electrical energy into the kinetic energy of an expelled mass; this formula measures the energy per second invested into the moving jet.
power-of-exhaust.interpretation: In the relation $P = \frac{1}{2} \dot{m} v_e^2$, $P$ is the mechanical jet power of the exhaust plume in watts ($\text{W}$), $\dot{m} = \frac{dm}{dt}$ denotes the propellant mass consumption rate in kilograms per second ($\text{kg}/\text{s}$), and $v_e$ represents the equivalent exhaust velocity relative to the nozzle exit plane in meters per second ($\text{m}/\text{s}$). The quadratic dependence on $v_e$ implies that high-specific-impulse engines (such as ion drives) require significantly greater input power per unit of thrust than low-velocity chemical thrusters.
power-of-exhaust.symmetry_origin: Derived from the conservation of energy (invariance under continuous time translations via Noether's theorem) applied to an open thermodynamic control volume with steady mass flow.
power-of-exhaust.limits_and_boundary: In the non-relativistic limit $v_e \ll c$, the classical kinetic energy expression is exact. In the limit $v_e \to 0$, jet power vanishes ($P \to 0$). For relativistic exhaust velocities where $v_e \sim c$, the equation must be replaced by the relativistic kinetic energy flux $P = (\gamma - 1) \dot{m} c^2$.

lagrangian-variation-displacement.title: Condition for Translational Invariance of the Lagrangian
lagrangian-variation-displacement.conceptual_definition: For a mechanical system described by a Lagrangian $L$ that depends on the positions $\mathbf{r}_i$ of $N$ particles, the principle of homogeneity of space dictates that the physics should be unchanged by a uniform shift of the entire system. This equation is the mathematical expression of that principle, stating that the total variation of the Lagrangian, $\delta L$, is zero when every particle is displaced by the same infinitesimal vector $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}$. Since $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}$ is arbitrary, this implies that the sum of the gradients of the Lagrangian with respect to each particle's position must be zero, $\sum_{i=1}^{N} \nabla_i L = 0$.
lagrangian-variation-displacement.intuitive_summary: If you move your entire experiment to a different spot in an empty room, the physical laws governing it shouldn't change. This equation is the mathematical way of saying that the system's fundamental description, the Lagrangian $L$, doesn't care about its absolute position in space. This property, when true, leads directly to the law of conservation of total momentum.
lagrangian-variation-displacement.symmetry_origin: This equation is a direct application of Noether's theorem. The continuous symmetry is the invariance of the Lagrangian under the group of spatial translations, reflecting the homogeneity of space. The corresponding conserved quantity is the total linear momentum of the system.
lagrangian-variation-displacement.limits_and_boundary: This principle is fundamental and holds across different physical regimes. In the classical limit ($\hbar \to 0$), it is a cornerstone of Lagrangian mechanics leading to momentum conservation. In the relativistic limit ($v \to c$), the principle extends to invariance under spacetime translations (the Poincaré group), where the conserved quantity is the energy-momentum four-vector. In quantum mechanics, the equivalent statement is that the Hamiltonian operator $\hat{H}$ commutes with the momentum operator $\hat{\mathbf{P}}$, i.e., $[\hat{H}, \hat{\mathbf{P}}] = 0$, ensuring that momentum is a conserved quantity if the system is translationally invariant.

variation-of-the-hamiltonian.title: Differential of Hamilton's Principal Function along an Extremal Trajectory
variation-of-the-hamiltonian.conceptual_definition: For a physical system traversing a classical on-shell trajectory (satisfying the Euler-Lagrange equations), the variation of the action functional $S(q, t)$ with respect to variations at the boundary coordinates $\delta q_i$ and boundary time $\delta t$ is given by $dS = \sum_i p_i dq_i - H dt$. This fundamental differential identity demonstrates that canonical momentum $p_i = \partial S / \partial q_i$ and the Hamiltonian $-H = \partial S / \partial t$ serve as the conjugate gradients of Hamilton's principal function.
variation-of-the-hamiltonian.intuitive_summary: When a path already minimizes the action, wiggling the intermediate trajectory produces no first-order change. The only change in action comes from shifting the endpoints in space (scaled by momentum $p_i$) or in time (scaled by negative energy $-H$).
variation-of-the-hamiltonian.interpretation: In the relation $\delta S = \sum p_i \delta q_i - H \delta t$, $\delta S$ represents the first-order differential of Hamilton's principal function evaluated along an extremal path. The term $p_i$ is the canonical momentum conjugate to the generalized coordinate $q_i$, such that $\sum p_i \delta q_i$ captures the spatial endpoint contribution. The term $H$ represents the Hamiltonian (total energy of the system), and $-H \delta t$ reflects the temporal endpoint variation arising from the Legendre transformation of the Lagrangian.
variation-of-the-hamiltonian.symmetry_origin: Rooted in temporal and spatial translation invariance via Noether's theorem; invariance under spatial translation implies constant conjugate momentum $p_i$, while invariance under time translation implies energy conservation ($dH/dt = -\partial L/\partial t = 0$).
variation-of-the-hamiltonian.limits_and_boundary: In the semiclassical limit $\hbar \to 0$, the quantum mechanical wave function takes the WKB form $\psi(q, t) \sim A \exp(i S / \hbar)$, where the phase gradient matches $\nabla S = \mathbf{p}$ and $-\partial_t S = E$, reproducing the classical differential relation.

scattering-amplitude-dyson-series.title: Scattering Amplitude via the Dyson Series
scattering-amplitude-dyson-series.equation: S_{fi} = \langle f | T \exp\left( -i \int \mathcal{H}_I(x) d^4 x \right) | i \rangle
scattering-amplitude-dyson-series.conceptual_definition: The scattering matrix element $S_{fi} = \langle f | S | i \rangle$ represents the probability amplitude for a system prepared in an asymptotic free initial state $|i\rangle$ at $t \to -\infty$ to be observed in a free final state $|f\rangle$ at $t \to +\infty$. The Dyson operator $S = T \exp\left( -i \int \mathcal{H}_I(x) \, d^4 x \right)$ evolves the system under the interaction Hamiltonian density $\mathcal{H}_I(x)$, where the time-ordering operator $T$ chronologically arranges non-commuting field operators.
scattering-amplitude-dyson-series.intuitive_summary: The Dyson series acts as a quantum movie projector: it takes non-interacting incoming wavepackets in the far past, sums up all possible chronological sequences of local interactions across spacetime, and computes the quantum overlap with the desired outgoing particles in the far future.
scattering-amplitude-dyson-series.interpretation: The quantity $S_{fi}$ is the complex scattering amplitude whose squared modulus $|S_{fi}|^2$ yields the transition probability. The bra $\langle f|$ and ket $|i\rangle$ denote asymptotic Fock states of free particle excitations in the interaction picture. The symbol $T$ represents the Dyson time-ordering operator, which ensures that field operators at later spacetime coordinates appear to the left of operators at earlier coordinates. The term $\mathcal{H}_I(x)$ is the interaction Hamiltonian density evaluated at the spacetime four-vector $x^\mu = (t, \mathbf{x})$, and $d^4 x = dt \, d^3x$ is the invariant four-volume element integrated over all Minkowski spacetime.
scattering-amplitude-dyson-series.symmetry_origin: Rooted in spacetime translation invariance and Lorentz symmetry (Poincaré group), which ensures four-momentum conservation during the scattering process, along with the unitarity requirement $S^\dagger S = \mathbf{1}$ arising from the conservation of quantum probability.
scattering-amplitude-dyson-series.limits_and_boundary: In the non-interacting limit where $\mathcal{H}_I(x) \to 0$, the $S$-matrix reduces to the identity operator, giving $S_{fi} \to \delta_{fi}$. In the perturbative weak-coupling regime, expanding the exponential yields the standard Feynman diagram series; non-perturbatively, the asymptotic states require wave-function renormalization via the Lehmann-Symanzik-Zimmermann (LSZ) reduction formula.

quantum-correlation-triangle-inequality.title: Monogamy of Entanglement (CKW Inequality)
quantum-correlation-triangle-inequality.conceptual_definition: The monogamy of entanglement is a property of multipartite quantum systems which constrains the distribution of entanglement. For a tripartite system $ABC$, if system $A$ is entangled with system $B$, this limits the extent to which $A$ can also be entangled with system $C$. The Coffman-Kundu-Wootters (CKW) inequality, $C^2_{AB} + C^2_{AC} \le C^2_{A(BC)}$, provides a precise quantitative statement of this principle for three-qubit systems, where $C$ is the entanglement measure known as concurrence.
quantum-correlation-triangle-inequality.intuitive_summary: Entanglement is a 'monogamous' resource. If a quantum particle, Alice, is maximally entangled with Bob, she cannot share any entanglement with a third particle, Charlie. The more she is 'committed' to Bob, the less she can be 'committed' to Charlie.
quantum-correlation-triangle-inequality.interpretation: In the inequality $C^2_{AB} + C^2_{AC} \le C^2_{A(BC)}$, the term $C^2_{AB}$ represents the squared concurrence, a measure of entanglement, between subsystems $A$ and $B$. Similarly, $C^2_{AC}$ is the squared concurrence between $A$ and $C$. The term on the right, $C^2_{A(BC)}$, represents the squared concurrence between subsystem $A$ and the composite system $(BC)$. This inequality, known as the CKW inequality, demonstrates that entanglement cannot be freely shared. The sum of bipartite entanglements of a single system with two others is bounded by the entanglement of that system with the pair, formalizing the concept of monogamy.
quantum-correlation-triangle-inequality.symmetry_origin: This inequality is not a consequence of a spacetime or gauge symmetry, but rather a structural property of the Hilbert space formalism for composite quantum systems. It arises from the properties of the tensor product and the mathematical definition of entanglement measures like concurrence.
quantum-correlation-triangle-inequality.limits_and_boundary: In the classical limit where $\hbar \to 0$, quantum entanglement vanishes, and this inequality becomes trivial or inapplicable as classical correlations are not monogamous. For example, a classical variable can be perfectly correlated with an arbitrary number of other variables. In the quantum case, if system $A$ is maximally entangled with $B$ (e.g., part of a Bell state), then $C_{AB}$ is maximal, which implies $C_{AC}$ must be zero. This means $A$ cannot be entangled with $C$ at all.

generalized-coordinate-in-classical-mech.title: Generalized Coordinate in Classical Mechanics
generalized-coordinate-in-classical-mech.description: A set of independent parameters that uniquely specify the spatial configuration of a constrained dynamical system in configuration space.
generalized-coordinate-in-classical-mech.conceptual_definition: A generalized coordinate $q_i$ is an element of an $n$-dimensional configuration manifold $\mathcal{Q}$, where $n = 3N - k$ corresponds to the degrees of freedom for a system of $N$ particles subject to $k$ holonomic constraints. The position vector of any particle $\mathbf{r}_j$ is expressed as a smooth function $\mathbf{r}_j = \mathbf{r}_j(q_1, q_2, \dots, q_n, t)$, thereby automatically embedding the geometric constraints into the parameterization.
generalized-coordinate-in-classical-mech.interpretation: The index $i \in \{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ specifies the degree of freedom. In Lagrangian mechanics, the state of a system evolves along a trajectory $q_i(t)$ governed by the Euler-Lagrange equations, while in Hamiltonian mechanics, $q_i$ pairs canonically with conjugate momentum $p_i$ to form coordinates $(q_i, p_i)$ on the symplectic phase space manifold $T^*\mathcal{Q}$.
generalized-coordinate-in-classical-mech.limits_and_boundary: In the limit where holonomic constraints $k \to 0$, the generalized coordinates $q_i$ reduce directly to standard Cartesian coordinates $\{x_j, y_j, z_j\}$. In the quantum limit $\hbar \to 0$, the coordinate operator $\hat{q}_i$ converges to the classical observable $q_i$ via the correspondence principle.
generalized-coordinate-in-classical-mech.symmetry_origin: Diffeomorphism invariance of the configuration manifold $\mathcal{Q}$ ensures that the laws of analytical mechanics remain form-invariant under arbitrary point transformations $q_i \to Q_i(q, t)$. If the Lagrangian is invariant under translations along $q_i$ (i.e., $\partial L / \partial q_i = 0$), the corresponding conjugate momentum $p_i$ is conserved via Noether's theorem.

non-relativistic-fermi-energy-f33a53c6.title: Non-Relativistic Fermi Energy
non-relativistic-fermi-energy-f33a53c6.description: Defines the Fermi energy as the chemical potential of a non-interacting Fermi gas at absolute zero, representing the maximum single-particle kinetic energy state occupied in the Fermi sea.
non-relativistic-fermi-energy-f33a53c6.conceptual_definition: The Fermi energy $E_F$ is the energy of the highest occupied single-particle quantum state in an ideal system of non-interacting fermions at absolute zero temperature ($T = 0\text{ K}$). In the non-relativistic parabolic dispersion regime where dispersion is given by $E(p) = p^2 / (2m)$, it corresponds directly to the kinetic energy evaluated at the Fermi momentum $p_F$, satisfying $E_F = p_F^2 / (2m) = \frac{\hbar^2}{2m}(3\pi^2 n)^{2/3}$ for a 3D gas of spin-$1/2$ fermions.
non-relativistic-fermi-energy-f33a53c6.interpretation: The quantity $E_F$ is the Fermi energy with SI units of Joules ($\text{J}$), often expressed in electron-volts ($\text{eV}$). It is determined by the particle mass $m$ and the Fermi momentum $p_F = \hbar (3\pi^2 n)^{1/3}$, where $\hbar$ is the reduced Planck constant and $n$ is the fermion number density. Unlike classical gases where kinetic energy vanishes as $T \to 0$, $E_F$ remains strictly positive due to quantum degeneracy, generating non-zero degeneracy pressure.
non-relativistic-fermi-energy-f33a53c6.limits_and_boundary: Valid in the non-relativistic limit where $E_F \ll m c^2$ (or $p_F \ll m c$). When particle density $n$ or momentum $p_F$ increases such that $E_F \sim m c^2$, the system transitions to the relativistic regime where $E_F \approx c p_F$. In the classical limit $\hbar \to 0$ or high-temperature dilute limit $k_B T \gg E_F$, quantum degeneracy effects vanish and Maxwell-Boltzmann statistics are recovered.
non-relativistic-fermi-energy-f33a53c6.symmetry_origin: Rooted in particle exchange antisymmetry under the permutation group $S_N$ (Pauli exclusion principle for fermions) combined with spatial translation invariance yielding momentum eigenstates.

critical-density-of-the-universe-1a76891.title: Critical Density of the Universe
critical-density-of-the-universe-1a76891.description: Defines the critical mass-energy density required for a spatially flat universe.
critical-density-of-the-universe-1a76891.conceptual_definition: The critical density, $\rho_c$, is the average mass-energy density of the universe required for it to be spatially flat (zero curvature). If the actual density is greater than $\rho_c$, the universe is closed and will eventually recollapse; if less, it is open and will expand forever. This value is crucial for understanding the geometry and ultimate fate of the cosmos.
critical-density-of-the-universe-1a76891.interpretation: This equation represents the threshold density that balances the expansion of the universe with the gravitational attraction of its contents. It is derived from the Friedmann equations, specifically for a spatially flat universe (zero curvature). The critical density is not a constant value but changes over cosmic time as the Hubble parameter evolves, though H_0 here refers to its present-day value. It serves as a fundamental reference point for cosmological models, particularly in the $\LambdaCDM$ model where the total density parameter is normalized to unity.
critical-density-of-the-universe-1a76891.limits_and_boundary: This formula is valid within the framework of General Relativity and the Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) metric, assuming a homogeneous and isotropic universe on large scales. It specifically applies to the present epoch when using the current Hubble constant H_0. It does not account for quantum gravitational effects or very early universe phenomena where different physics might dominate.
critical-density-of-the-universe-1a76891.symmetry_origin: The formula originates from the Friedmann equations, which are derived from Einstein's field equations under the assumption of a homogeneous and isotropic universe (FLRW metric). These assumptions embody spatial symmetries, specifically translational and rotational invariance on cosmological scales. The underlying principle is the conservation of energy and momentum within the expanding spacetime.

squared-probability-amplitude-5a63ee7b.title: Squared Probability Amplitude
squared-probability-amplitude-5a63ee7b.description: This expression represents the squared magnitude of the probability amplitude for a quantum system in state \Psi to be found in a specific eigenstate \phi_i.
squared-probability-amplitude-5a63ee7b.conceptual_definition: In quantum mechanics, the state of a system is described by a state vector $\Psi$ in a Hilbert space. An observable quantity corresponds to a Hermitian operator, and its possible measurement outcomes are the eigenvalues of that operator, with corresponding eigenstates $\phi_i$. The inner product $\langle \phi_i$ | $\Psi \rangle$ is the probability amplitude that a measurement will yield the eigenvalue associated with $\phi_i$.
squared-probability-amplitude-5a63ee7b.interpretation: The value |$\langle \phi_i$ | $\Psi \rangle$|^2 quantifies the probability of observing the system in the state $\phi_i$ when a measurement is performed on the system initially in state $\Psi$. It is a real, non-negative number between 0 and 1, representing the likelihood of a specific measurement outcome. This is the core of the Born Rule, stating that the probability of a particular outcome is the square of the absolute value of the probability amplitude.
squared-probability-amplitude-5a63ee7b.limits_and_boundary: The value is always non-negative and less than or equal to 1. If $\Psi$ is orthogonal to $\phi_i$, the value is 0, meaning no probability of finding the system in state $\phi_i$. If $\Psi$ is identical to $\phi_i$ (and normalized), the value is 1, meaning certainty. The sum over all possible orthogonal states $\phi_i$ must equal 1, reflecting the normalization of the state vector $\Psi$.
squared-probability-amplitude-5a63ee7b.symmetry_origin: This expression is inherently tied to the probabilistic interpretation of quantum mechanics, which itself is a postulate. It respects the unitary evolution of quantum states, as unitary transformations preserve inner products and thus probabilities. The normalization of the state vector, $\langle \Psi$ | $\Psi \rangle$ = 1, is a fundamental symmetry ensuring total probability is conserved.

holonomic-constraint-equation-0860cfae.title: Holonomic Constraint Equation
holonomic-constraint-equation-0860cfae.description: An algebraic relation restricting the generalized coordinates and time of a dynamical system to a sub-manifold of configuration space.
holonomic-constraint-equation-0860cfae.conceptual_definition: A holonomic constraint is an algebraic or finite condition of the form $f(q_1, q_2, \dots, q_n, t) = 0$ that limits the kinematically accessible configurations of a classical mechanical system. Constraints that explicitly depend on time $t$ are termed rheonomic, while those independent of time are scleronomic.
holonomic-constraint-equation-0860cfae.interpretation: In this equation, $f$ represents the scalar constraint function whose zero level-set defines the configuration hypersurface. The coordinates $q_i$ denote the set of generalized coordinates parameterizing the system, and $t$ represents time. When $k$ independent holonomic constraints of this form are present in a system of $n$ generalized coordinates, the effective physical degrees of freedom are reduced to $n - k$.
holonomic-constraint-equation-0860cfae.limits_and_boundary: In the limit $\partial f / \partial t \to 0$, the constraint becomes scleronomic ($f(q_i) = 0$), conserving the Jacobi energy. In the rigid-body limit where interparticle distances $|\mathbf{r}_i - \mathbf{r}_j| = c_{ij}$, the system reduces to six macroscopic degrees of freedom.
holonomic-constraint-equation-0860cfae.symmetry_origin: Diffeomorphism invariance on the configuration manifold $\mathcal{Q}$; time-translation invariance is broken if $\partial f / \partial t \neq 0$ (rheonomic), precluding energy conservation.

holonomic-constraint-equation-0860cfae.intuitive_summary: A geometric rule that confines a system's motion to a designated curve, surface, or hypersurface in configuration space, reducing its effective degrees of freedom.

commutativity-of-gradient-and-time-deriv.title: Commutativity of Gradient and Time Derivative
commutativity-of-gradient-and-time-deriv.description: This equation demonstrates the commutativity of the gradient spatial derivative operator and the partial time derivative operator when applied to a scalar field.
commutativity-of-gradient-and-time-deriv.conceptual_definition: The equation $\nabla (\frac{\partial \Lambda}{\partial t}) = \frac{\partial}{\partial t} ( \nabla \Lambda)$ asserts that the order of applying a spatial gradient and a temporal derivative to a scalar field $\Lambda$ does not affect the final result. This property, known as commutativity, holds true for sufficiently smooth fields where the mixed partial derivatives are continuous. It implies that the rate of change of the spatial variation of a field is identical to the spatial variation of its rate of change.
commutativity-of-gradient-and-time-deriv.interpretation: Physically, this identity means that observing how the spatial distribution of a scalar field changes over time (left side) is equivalent to observing the spatial distribution of the field's temporal evolution (right side). In the context of electromagnetism, where $\Lambda$ might represent a scalar potential, this commutativity is crucial for simplifying expressions and demonstrating consistency in field equations. It underpins the mathematical rigor required for deriving wave equations or ensuring gauge invariance, allowing for flexible manipulation of differential operators.
commutativity-of-gradient-and-time-deriv.limits_and_boundary: This identity holds for scalar fields $\Lambda(x,y,z,t)$ that are at least twice continuously differentiable with respect to both spatial coordinates and time. This condition ensures that the order of differentiation does not matter, as per Schwarz's theorem on the equality of mixed partial derivatives. It is a fundamental mathematical identity and does not typically have physical boundary conditions in itself, but rather applies within domains where $\Lambda$ is sufficiently smooth.
commutativity-of-gradient-and-time-deriv.symmetry_origin: This identity is a consequence of the fundamental properties of partial differential operators and the independence of spatial and temporal coordinates in standard Euclidean and Minkowski spacetime (when considering non-relativistic or special relativistic contexts where time and space are distinct dimensions). It reflects the mathematical fact that mixed partial derivatives commute for sufficiently smooth functions, which is a property inherent to the structure of differentiable manifolds.

cosmic-photon-emission-observation-time-.title: Cosmic Photon Emission-Observation Time Mapping
cosmic-photon-emission-observation-time-.description: Represents the temporal correspondence and null-geodesic mapping between the cosmic epoch of photon emission $t_{\text{em}}$ and the cosmic epoch of reception $t_{\text{ob}}$ in an expanding Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) spacetime.
cosmic-photon-emission-observation-time-.conceptual_definition: In standard cosmological models governed by the Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) metric $ds^2 = -c^2 dt^2 + a(t)^2 d\Sigma^2$, radially propagating photons travel along null geodesics ($ds^2 = 0$). The propagation between a distant source emitting radiation at cosmic time $t_{\text{em}}$ and a comoving observer receiving it at cosmic time $t_{\text{ob}}$ establishes a bijective mapping $t_{\text{ob}} \to t_{\text{em}}$ parameterized by the comoving coordinate distance $\chi = c \int_{t_{\text{em}}}^{t_{\text{ob}}} \frac{dt}{a(t)}$.
cosmic-photon-emission-observation-time-.interpretation: The symbol $t_{\text{ob}}$ denotes the cosmic observation time (typically the current cosmic age $t_0$), while $t_{\text{em}}$ denotes the earlier cosmic time of photon emission. The relation encapsulates cosmological lookback time and time dilation of cosmic signals, where the frequency shift is tied directly to the evolution of the cosmic scale factor $a(t)$ across the interval $[t_{\text{em}}, t_{\text{ob}}]$.
cosmic-photon-emission-observation-time-.limits_and_boundary: In the local limit where the comoving separation vanishes ($\chi \to 0$), $t_{\text{ob}} - t_{\text{em}} \to 0$. In the asymptotic limit approaching the cosmic singularity, as $t_{\text{em}} \to 0$, the scale factor $a(t_{\text{em}}) \to 0$, leading to infinite cosmological redshift $z \to \infty$.
cosmic-photon-emission-observation-time-.symmetry_origin: Rooted in the spatial homogeneity and isotropy of the FLRW spacetime metric (isometry group $\mathrm{SO}(3) \ltimes \mathbb{R}^3$ or $\mathrm{SO}(1,3)$ / $\mathrm{SO}(4)$ depending on spatial curvature) and conformal invariance along null geodesics.
